transcription.tex: 1. For each graph, find its gradient and the shaded area.
\[\begin{array}{c|ccc}&a&b&c\\\text{Gradient}&3&2&-1.5\\\text{Area}&73.5&150&26.25\end{array}\]
2. A car travels for 45 minutes at an average speed of 35 mph. Find the distance.
\[d=35\times\frac{45}{60}=26.25\text{ miles}.\]
Adding twice the first equation to the second gives \(7x=14\). Thus \(x=2\), \(y=-1.5\).
4. Solve \(2x^2+3x-7=0\) to 3 significant figures.

transcription.tex: \textbf{Displacement–time graphs}\par Describe each graph: a horizontal line; a rising straight line; a rising curve whose gradient increases.
Horizontal: stationary.\par Rising straight line: constant positive velocity.\par Increasing positive gradient: positive acceleration.

\textbf{Velocity is the gradient}\[v=\frac{ds}{dt}\] \[\text{Average velocity}=\frac{\text{displacement}}{\text{time}}\] \[\text{Average speed}=\frac{\text{total distance}}{\text{time}}\] Returning to the starting point gives zero overall displacement, even when the distance travelled is not zero.

sourceMapping.method: Native text and LaTeX draft; explicit question/answer objects

transcription.tex: A cyclist travels 5 km in a straight line in 20 minutes, waits for half an hour, then returns in 15 minutes. Find each stage’s average velocity, the whole journey’s average velocity, and its average speed.
Overall displacement is zero, so average velocity is zero.\[\text{Average speed}=\frac{10}{65/60}=9.23\text{ km/h}.\]

sourceMapping.method: Native text and LaTeX draft; explicit question/answer objects

transcription.tex: 2. Khalid drives from home towards a hotel for 2.5 hours at an average velocity of 60 km/h, stops for lunch, then continues. The graph uses equal vertical divisions.\par a. Find the hotel’s displacement from home.\par b. Find the average velocity for the journey.
First stage: \(60\times2.5=150\) km. Each square represents \(150/6=25\) km.\[s=7.5\times25=187.5\text{ km}.\]

sourceMapping.method: Native text and LaTeX draft; explicit question/answer objects

transcription.tex: 3. Sarah cycles north from home at 10:00. Use the displacement–time graph.\par a. Find her velocity from 10:00 to 11:00.\par b. Estimate when she passes home on the return.\par c. Find the last two stage velocities.\par d. Find her average speed overall.
\[v=12/1=12\text{ km/h north}.\]
The return velocity is \(-10\) km/h, so 12 km takes 1.2 hours. She passes home at about 12:42 (approximately 12:45 from the sketch).
\[v_3=\frac{-3-12}{1.5}=-10\text{ km/h}\]\[v_4=3\text{ km/h}.\] \[\text{Average speed}=30/4=7.5\text{ km/h}.\]

sourceMapping.method: Native text and LaTeX draft; explicit question/answer objects

transcription.tex: 4. A ball is thrown vertically upwards and returns to the ground. Use its displacement–time graph.\par a. Find the maximum height and its time.\par b. State the velocity at the highest point.\par c. Describe the motion before and after the highest point.
Maximum height: 2.5 m at 0.75 s. At the highest point, the graph has zero gradient, so velocity is \(0\text{ m/s}\).

Before the highest point, velocity is positive and decreases to zero. Afterwards velocity is negative and becomes more negative: the ball speeds up downwards. With no air resistance, it returns to the launch height with the same speed as at launch.

transcription.tex: \textbf{Velocity–time graphs}\par A line on the time axis means stationary. A horizontal line above the axis means constant positive velocity. A rising straight line means constant positive acceleration.

\textbf{Gradient and area}\[a=\frac{dv}{dt}\] Signed area under a velocity–time graph gives displacement.\par To find total distance, add the magnitudes of areas above and below the time axis.\par Area under a speed–time graph gives distance. These coincide only when the velocity does not change sign.

transcription.tex: A cyclist travels at 6 m/s for 8 s, then decelerates uniformly to rest over 4 s. Find her displacement and deceleration.
\[s=6\times8+\tfrac12\times4\times6=60\text{ m}.\]
\[a=\frac{0-6}{4}=-1.5\text{ m/s}^2.\] Deceleration is \(1.5\text{ m/s}^2\).

sourceMapping.method: Native text and LaTeX draft; explicit question/answer objects

transcription.tex: A particle accelerates uniformly from rest to 8 m/s in \(T\) s, stays at 8 m/s for \(5T\) s, then decelerates uniformly to rest over 40 s.\par a. Sketch the velocity–time graph.\par b. Given total displacement 600 m, find \(T\).
Join \((0,0),(T,8),(6T,8),(6T+40,0)\) with straight lines. The middle section is horizontal.
\[\tfrac12(8)T+8(5T)+\tfrac12(8)(40)=600\] \[44T+160=600\quad\Rightarrow\quad T=10\text{ s}.\]

sourceMapping.method: Native text and LaTeX draft; explicit question/answer objects

transcription.tex: A car travels 2145 m in 120 s. It accelerates uniformly from rest for 30 s to 22 m/s, maintains this for \(T\) s, then decelerates uniformly to rest.\par a. Sketch its speed–time graph.\par b. Find \(T\).\par A motorcycle starts 10 s later from the same point, accelerating uniformly from rest. It passes the car 990 m from the start while the car is travelling at 22 m/s.\par c. Find the motorcycle’s journey time to that point.\par d. Find its acceleration.
The car travels \(\tfrac12(30)(22)=330\) m initially.\[t_{\rm car}=30+\frac{990-330}{22}=60\text{ s}.\] Motorcycle time \(=60-10=50\) s.
\[990=\tfrac12a(50)^2\Rightarrow a=0.792\text{ m/s}^2.\]

sourceMapping.method: Native text and LaTeX draft; explicit question/answer objects

transcription.tex: A car travels at 20 m/s for 25 s, decelerates at \(0.4\text{ m/s}^2\) to 8 m/s, stays at 8 m/s for 60 s, then accelerates uniformly to 20 m/s. The total distance is 1960 m.\par a. Sketch the speed–time graph.\par b. Find the deceleration time.\par c. Find the total journey time.
Deceleration time \(=(20-8)/0.4=30\) s.\par Join \((0,20),(25,20),(55,8)\),\par then \((115,8),(115+t,20)\), where \(t\) is the final stage duration.

transcription.tex: 8. A motorcyclist and car start from rest at the same junction at the same time. The motorcyclist accelerates at \(3\text{ m/s}^2\) for 8 s, then keeps a constant velocity. The car accelerates uniformly to 30 m/s in 20 s, then maintains this velocity.\par a. Sketch both velocity–time graphs.\par b. The car passes the motorcyclist by a pedestrian. Find the pedestrian’s distance from the junction.
Motorcyclist: \((0,0)\) to \((8,24)\), then horizontal. Car: \((0,0)\) to \((20,30)\), then horizontal.

transcription.tex: \textbf{Constant-acceleration equations}\par \(s\): displacement; \(u\): initial velocity; \(v\): final velocity; \(a\): constant acceleration; \(t\): duration.\par Use a consistent positive direction and the same time interval for every quantity.
Derive two equations using the straight velocity–time graph.
Gradient: \[a=\frac{v-u}{t}\Rightarrow v=u+at.\] Signed trapezium area: \[s=\frac{u+v}{2}t.\]

transcription.tex: A particle passes \(A\) at 8 m/s and decelerates at \(1.5\text{ m/s}^2\). It reaches \(B\) at 2 m/s. Find:\par a. the time from \(A\) to \(B\);\par b. the distance \(AB\).\par It continues with the same acceleration and reaches \(C\) 6 s after passing \(A\). Find:\par c. its velocity at \(C\);\par d. its displacement from \(A\) and total distance travelled.
\[2=8-1.5t\Rightarrow t=4\text{ s}.\] \[AB=\tfrac12(8+2)4=20\text{ m}.\]

transcription.tex: 9. A skier travels straight up a hill at 16 m/s and decelerates uniformly to rest over 40 s. Find:\par a. the deceleration;\par b. the distance travelled.
\[a=(0-16)/40=-0.4\text{ m/s}^2.\] Deceleration is \(0.4\text{ m/s}^2\).

transcription.tex: 11. A particle travels from \(A\) to \(B\) with acceleration \(1.5\text{ m/s}^2\) for 12 s, then from \(B\) to \(C\) with a different constant acceleration for 10 s. Velocities at \(A,C\) are 1 and 43 m/s. Find:\par a. the velocity at \(B\);\par b. the acceleration from \(B\) to \(C\);\par c. the distance \(AC\).

sourceMapping.method: Native text and LaTeX draft; explicit question/answer objects

transcription.tex: 12. A cyclist accelerates uniformly from rest to 5 m/s over 20 s at \(x\text{ m/s}^2\). She then decelerates uniformly to rest at \(\tfrac12x\text{ m/s}^2\). Find:\par a. \(x\);\par b. the total distance.
Deceleration \(=0.125\text{ m/s}^2\), so stopping time \(=5/0.125=40\) s.\[d=\tfrac12(5)(20)+\tfrac12(5)(40)=150\text{ m}.\]

sourceMapping.method: Native text and LaTeX draft; explicit question/answer objects

transcription.tex: 13. A particle passes \(A,B,C\) at 20, 30 and 45 m/s with constant acceleration. The times from \(A\) to \(B\) and \(B\) to \(C\) are \(t_1,t_2\).\par a. Show that \(t_1/t_2=2/3\).\par b. Given \(t_1+t_2=50\) s, find \(AB\).
\[t_2=\tfrac32t_1\Rightarrow\tfrac52t_1=50\Rightarrow t_1=20.\] \[AB=\tfrac12(20+30)20=500\text{ m}.\]

sourceMapping.method: Native text and LaTeX draft; explicit question/answer objects

transcription.tex: \textbf{Eliminate time}\[s=\frac{u+v}{2}\frac{v-u}{a}\]
\textbf{Eliminate final velocity}\[s=\frac{u+(u+at)}2t\]
\[s=ut+\tfrac12at^2.\]
\textbf{Eliminate initial velocity}\[s=\frac{(v-at)+v}{2}t\]
\[s=vt-\tfrac12at^2.\] All these equations require constant acceleration.

transcription.tex: 1. A particle accelerates at \(5\text{ m/s}^2\) from 3 to 18 m/s. Find the distance.
2. A particle passes \(O\) at 13 m/s towards \(A\), where \(OA=20\) m, with acceleration \(-4\text{ m/s}^2\). Find the times at \(A\) and the return time to \(O\).
\[20=13t-2t^2\Rightarrow(2t-5)(t-4)=0\] \[t=2.5\text{ s or }4\text{ s}.\] \[0=13t-2t^2\Rightarrow t=0\text{ or }6.5.\] It returns to \(O\) after 6.5 s.

sourceMapping.method: Native text and LaTeX draft; explicit question/answer objects

transcription.tex: A lorry passes \(A\) at \(u\) m/s and \(B\) at 34 m/s, 10 s later, with constant acceleration. Given \(AB=240\) m, find:\par a. \(u\);\par b. the time from \(A\) to the midpoint of \(AB\).
\[240=\tfrac12(u+34)10\Rightarrow u=14\text{ m/s}.\]
\[a=(34-14)/10=2\text{ m/s}^2\] \[120=14t+t^2\Rightarrow(t+20)(t-6)=0.\] The positive time is \(6\) s.

sourceMapping.method: Native text and LaTeX draft; explicit question/answer objects

transcription.tex: 11. A particle passes the origin at 12 m/s with acceleration \(-5\text{ m/s}^2\). Find the times at \(x=8\) m and the velocity at \(x=-8\) m.
12. Another particle passes the origin at 14 m/s with acceleration \(-4\text{ m/s}^2\). Find the difference between its times at \(x=22.5\) m and the total distance travelled between them.
\[22.5=14t-2t^2\Rightarrow t=2.5,\ 4.5\text{ s}.\] Difference: 2 s. Turning displacement \(=14^2/8=24.5\) m.\[d=2(24.5-22.5)=4\text{ m}.\]

transcription.tex: 15. An orienteer passes checkpoints \(P,Q,R\) in a straight line with constant acceleration. \(PQ=2.4\) km and \(QR=11.5\) km. The corresponding times are 1 hour and 1.5 hours. Find her acceleration and speed at \(P\).
Use km and hours. If initial speed is \(u\):\[2.4=u+\tfrac12a\] \[13.9=2.5u+\tfrac12a(2.5)^2.\]

transcription.tex: \textbf{Vertical motion under gravity}\par Model the body as a particle and neglect air resistance. Near Earth, use \(g=9.8\text{ m/s}^2\), unless the question specifies another value.\par Acceleration is downward throughout the flight, including at the highest point.

\textbf{Choose a positive direction}\par Up positive: \(a=-g\). Down positive: \(a=+g\).\par At the highest point, \(v=0\); the acceleration is still downward.\par Keep unrounded values during calculation and round final answers as the question requests.\par The constant-acceleration equations apply separately to each uninterrupted stage.

sourceMapping.method: Native text and LaTeX draft; explicit question/answer objects

transcription.tex: A book falls from rest from a shelf 1.4 m above a floor. Find:\par a. the time to reach the floor;\par b. its impact speed. Neglect air resistance.
Take downwards positive.\[1.4=\tfrac12(9.8)t^2\Rightarrow t=\sqrt{1.4/4.9}=0.535\text{ s}.\]
\[v^2=2(9.8)(1.4)\Rightarrow v=5.24\text{ m/s}.\] To 2 significant figures: 0.53 s and 5.2 m/s.

sourceMapping.method: Native text and LaTeX draft; explicit question/answer objects

transcription.tex: A ball is projected upwards at 21 m/s from a point 7 m above the ground. Neglect air resistance. Find:\par a. the greatest height above the ground;\par b. the time of flight.
At the highest point \(v=0\):\[0=21^2-2(9.8)s\Rightarrow s=22.5\text{ m}.\] Height above ground \(=22.5+7=29.5\) m.
At the ground, displacement from launch is \(-7\) m.\[-7=21t-4.9t^2\] The positive root is \(t=4.60\) s (3 s.f.).

transcription.tex: 10. A particle is projected upwards at 24.5 m/s. Find the total time it is at least 21 m above its launch point.
\[21=24.5t-4.9t^2\] The roots are \(1.0985\ldots\) and \(3.9015\ldots\).\[\Delta t=2.80\text{ s}.\]
11. A particle is projected upwards at \(u\) m/s. After 2 s it is still rising at \(u/3\) m/s. Find \(u\) and the time to return to the launch point.
\[u/3=u-9.8(2)\Rightarrow u=29.4\text{ m/s}.\] \[0=29.4t-4.9t^2\Rightarrow t=6\text{ s}\quad(t>0).\]

sourceMapping.method: Native text and LaTeX draft; explicit question/answer objects

transcription.tex: 12. Ball \(A\) is thrown downwards at 5 m/s from a tower 46 m high. Simultaneously ball \(B\) is thrown upwards from the ground at 18 m/s. Find the distance from the top of the tower to their collision point. Neglect air resistance.
\[s_A=5t+4.9t^2,\quad s_B=18t-4.9t^2\] \[s_A+s_B=46\Rightarrow23t=46\Rightarrow t=2\text{ s}.\]
\[s_A=5(2)+4.9(2)^2=29.6\text{ m}.\] This is measured downwards from the tower top.
